title: Secondary Complications 5–13
source_document: English Master Data Collection & Clinical Content Repository

items: Spasticity: Vel-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes resulting from upper motor neuron loss. Can cause involuntary muscle spasms, pain, and functional impairment, though mild spasticity may assist transfers and circulation.
Contractures: Permanent muscle/tendon shortening resulting from sustained immobility and spasticity, leading to loss of passive Range of Motion (ROM).
Neuropathic Pain: Arises from damaged neural tissue. Characterized as burning, shooting, stabbing, or electric-shock-like sensations occurring above, at, or below the injury level.

Musculoskeletal Pain: Originates from mechanical overload, altered body mechanics, and overuse injuries, particularly in the shoulders, wrists, and neck during transfers and manual wheelchair propulsion.
Pathophysiology: Loss of intercostal and abdominal muscle innervation (C1–T12) impairs inspiratory capacity and cough effectiveness.
Complications: Atelectasis, hypoventilation, and neurogenic pulmonary edema. Respiratory complications, including pneumonia, can be serious and require prompt medical management.
Risk Factors: Venous stasis from lower extremity paralysis, altered hypercoagulable state post-trauma, and vascular trauma.
Clinical Features: Asymmetrical lower limb swelling, localized warmth, erythema. Sudden onset shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxia indicate life-threatening PE.
Sublesional Osteoporosis: Rapid loss of bone mineral density (BMD) occurring below the level of injury due to the lack of mechanical weight-bearing loads and altered neurovascular signaling.
Risk: High susceptibility to low-energy fragility fractures, particularly around the distal femur and proximal tibia.
Psychological Reactions: Elevated incidence of major depressive disorder, anxiety, situational adjustment disorders, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Clinical Necessity: Requires routine integration of psychological screening, coping frameworks, peer mentorship, and cognitive behavioral interventions into long-term management.

Impact & Adaptation: Spinal cord injury alters reflex and psychogenic sexual responses, arousal, and sensation. Reproductive capability remains intact for most women (with temporary amenorrhea post-injury), while men may experience erectile or ejaculatory changes that can be managed with medical interventions.

Professional Support: Confidential counseling with urologists, gynecologists, and rehabilitation specialists provides guidance on fertility options, adaptive intimacy techniques, and safe family planning.
Definition & Symptoms: A sudden drop in blood pressure occurring when moving from a lying to a seated or standing position. Symptoms include lightheadedness, dizziness, blurred vision, or fainting.
Management: Gradual positional changes, abdominal binders, compression stockings, adequate fluid intake, and clinical evaluation by a healthcare provider.
Autonomic Disruption: Reduced ability to regulate body temperature below the injury level due to loss of sweating and shivering responses.

Risk Management: Protect against extreme environmental temperatures (hyperthermia in hot conditions, hypothermia in cold conditions) through appropriate clothing, hydration, and climate-controlled environments.
